overview: This card covers the atlas's modern Georgia record, not medieval georgia, despite the imported alias Kingdom of Georgia. Its 1994-2020 feature omits Sukhumi in Abkhazia yet includes Tskhinvali in South Ossetia; the modern feature includes both. Because these snapshots mix claimed territory with uneven omissions, they cannot show effective control. The approximate 1994 onset also trails restored independence by three years and UN admission by two.

periods.title: Independence, conflict and state rebuilding
periods.summary: Georgia restored independence in 1991, entered the UN in 1992 and faced violent power struggles and wars in South Ossetia and Abkhazia.

periods.title: Constitutional state under Shevardnadze
periods.summary: The 1995 Constitution organized a continuing independent state whose territorial claims exceeded the government's effective reach.

periods.title: Rose Revolution and reform era
periods.summary: A deeply flawed 2003 election triggered mass protests, Shevardnadze's resignation and a peaceful transfer to a new reforming leadership.

periods.title: War and postwar effective control
periods.summary: The August 2008 war ended active hostilities under a ceasefire, after which Russia exercised effective control in South Ossetia and Abkhazia.

periods.title: Ballot-box transfer and EU candidacy
periods.summary: The 2012 election produced Georgia's first peaceful transfer through the ballot box; the EU granted candidate status in December 2023.

periods.title: Contested election and stalled EU path
periods.summary: Observers documented serious pressure and rights concerns in 2024, while EU institutions described the accession process as halted and at a standstill.

sections.title: A modern state older than its atlas record

items.text: Georgia's Supreme Council proclaimed restoration of state independence on 9 April 1991, drawing authority from the 31 March referendum and the 26 May 1918 independence act. That legal language presents modern Georgia as restored, not created from nothing. It also makes the atlas's approximate 1994 onset three years late. Soviet Georgia and medieval Georgian kingdoms are essential antecedents, but neither is the state record described by georgia-1994.

The United Nations admitted the Republic of Georgia on 31 July 1992. Admission came after independence and before the atlas onset, so none of those three dates should be substituted for another. The country's commonly used English name later became simply Georgia, while the UN membership continued. A seat at the UN established international membership; it did not end civil conflict or give Tbilisi effective control over every claimed district.

Conflict around South Ossetia began before independence and reached a ceasefire in 1992. War in Abkhazia followed in 1992-1993, driving more than 200,000 ethnic Georgians from Abkhazia according to the UN profile. These were not tidy border edits: people lost homes, neighbours and access to family places. The 1994 atlas polygon's exclusion of Sukhumi but inclusion of Tskhinvali therefore cannot be a consistent picture of actual control.

Georgia adopted its Constitution on 24 August 1995. Article 1 calls Georgia an independent, unified and indivisible state and grounds statehood in the 1991 referendum and independence act. That is the constitutional claim to territory, not a claim that the government physically administered Abkhazia or South Ossetia in 1995. A careful map lesson keeps constitutional borders, diplomatic recognition and effective control in separate columns.

Active hostilities between Georgia and Russia ran from 8 to 12 August 2008. The European Court of Human Rights found that after the 12 August ceasefire Russia exercised effective control over South Ossetia, Abkhazia and initially a buffer zone, with control continuing in the two regions after withdrawal from the buffer. The judgment assigns Convention responsibility; it does not transfer sovereignty or make the atlas polygons a legal settlement.

A 2023 European Court judgment described Abkhazia as outside the Georgian government's de facto control and under Russia's continued effective control. In April 2024 the Court found a pattern of violations from hardened boundary lines around Abkhazia and South Ossetia since 2009, including blocked access to homes, land, relatives and Georgian-language education; it ruled on compensation in October 2025. The boundaries affect school mornings and family visits, not just diplomats' vocabulary.

The November 2003 parliamentary election was marred by serious irregularities. Large peaceful protests followed, Eduard Shevardnadze resigned and the proportional election result was cancelled. The change became known as the Rose Revolution. Its peaceful transfer was a major political achievement, but the election failure that triggered it matters too: a revolution named for flowers still began with citizens believing the ballot count was broken.

In 2012 the Georgian Dream coalition defeated the governing party, President Mikheil Saakashvili conceded and observers called it Georgia's first peaceful transfer of power through the ballot box. The same report described a polarized campaign, abuse concerns and an uneven playing field. Peaceful concession was a democratic milestone; it did not magically turn institutions, media or campaigning into a finished project.

The European Union granted Georgia candidate status on 14 December 2023. By June 2024, however, EU institutions said government actions had effectively halted the accession process; the official EU overview later described it as remaining at a standstill. Candidate status was a diplomatic achievement built over years, while the halt shows that a status label is conditional and can coexist with sharp concern about democratic direction.

OSCE observers' final report on the October 2024 parliamentary election documented voter pressure, weakened institutional independence, limits on fundamental freedoms and post-election protest suppression. It said these problems compromised the ability to vote without fear. The report does not itself cancel an election; it supplies evidence for judging its quality. Elections are more than boxes and paper: voters must be able to choose without wondering who is watching.

sections.title: Alphabets, bread, songs and a buried giant jar

items.text: An authentic modern sample is საქართველოს სახელმწიფოებრივი დამოუკიდებლობის აღდგენის აქტი, the official title meaning “Act of Restoration of State Independence of Georgia.” It is written in Mkhedruli, the rounded Georgian script used for most modern secular writing. This 1991 legal phrase is not medieval calligraphy and not a sample of Russian from the Soviet period. A different alphabet is visible before the reader translates a single word.

Georgia's writing tradition has three related systems: Mrgvlovani, Nuskhuri and Mkhedruli. Modern schools mainly teach Mkhedruli, while older forms survive especially in church use, manuscripts, stonework and artistic practice. Families, teachers, clergy and craftspeople all help transmit them. Kid challenge: Georgian has no capital-letter version waiting to shout at you; emphasis must find other tricks. That playful observation applies to modern Mkhedruli typography, not every historical convention.

Georgian wheat culture links fields, stone mills, ovens and special breads. Families and neighbours pass on local knowledge about seed, planting, harvest and baking; particular breads may mark births, weddings and funerals. UNESCO inscribed the tradition in 2025. It does not mean every Georgian grows wheat or follows identical rituals, but it shows how daily food can carry agricultural science, memory and family responsibility in one delicious package.

Georgian polyphonic singing layers independent voices instead of putting everyone on one tune. Regional forms accompany work, feasts, festivals and older healing customs. One western technique, krimanchuli, uses a high yodelling voice whose name evokes a cockerel's crow. It is a marvelous sound and an endangered social skill: UNESCO notes that rural migration and shrinking performance settings have weakened everyday transmission.

A qvevri is a large egg-shaped clay vessel buried in the ground. Families and neighbours traditionally press grapes, seal juice and skins inside, and leave fermentation and ageing for roughly five or six months. Children may learn pottery, farming and family ritual by watching and helping, while the wine itself is for adults. Fun fact: the vessel is basically a giant underground ceramic egg, but opening one early would ruin more than a surprise.

A bilingual preschool programme launched in 2020 was working in 34 kindergartens in minority-populated regions by 2024. Teachers use Georgian alongside children's Armenian or Azerbaijani home languages, helping pupils enter school without treating family language as a problem to erase. Thirty-four kindergartens are a meaningful start, not national completion; training, materials and family trust determine whether bilingual learning works beyond a pilot classroom.

Georgia introduced a universal health coverage programme in 2013, expanding publicly financed access and reducing some direct household burden. The 2023 health-system review still found low public spending, co-payments, costly outpatient medicines and unequal access. The achievement is a national coverage platform; the limitation is that “covered” can still leave a family choosing between a prescription and another bill.

Georgia launched a national hepatitis C elimination programme in 2015. By January 2023 WHO reported more than 2.8 million people screened, more than 80,000 treated and a cure rate above 99 percent among those treated. That is a striking public-health and laboratory achievement. It does not mean hepatitis vanished: finding undiagnosed infections, preventing reinfection and reaching every community remain part of elimination.

By October 2025, 60 rural clinics had telemedicine equipment linking patients and local staff with distant specialists. The equipment can reduce a mountain journey for advice or help detect a problem earlier. WHO also emphasized unfinished legal rules, stable financing, training and integration into routine care. A video screen is not a doctor teleportation portal; it works only when people, referrals, medicines and follow-up exist around it.

UNICEF's 2025 situation analysis reported E. coli contamination in drinking water for 24.9 percent of sampled households and functional, clean sanitation in only 16.7 percent of surveyed public schools, with rural and poorer children at greater risk. Those are survey findings, not a claim about every tap or toilet. Still, a school toilet is only a service when it has water, privacy, cleaning and safe waste handling; a porcelain bowl alone deserves no medal.

At Dmanisi, archaeologists found hominin remains, stone tools and extinct animals about 1.8 million years old, among the earliest well-dated evidence of humans outside Africa. A field museum lets visitors see research where discoveries were made, and educational work trains new learners. The modern Georgian state helps protect and study the site; it did not create the ancient people, and those hominins cannot honestly be issued modern Georgian passports after 1.8 million years.

ending.text: Georgia continues as a UN member state claiming Abkhazia and South Ossetia within its internationally recognized borders. The Georgian government still lacks de facto control in those regions, where Russian effective control and hardened boundary lines continue to shape daily life. The medieval kingdom, Soviet republic and 1991 restoration belong in the background, while the atlas's open georgia-1994 interval records modern-state continuity rather than predicting a final territorial settlement.
